paper_title: Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. Its LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache's.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context decoding by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only subset of the sequence, chosen by fixed pattern or learned per query. Recent production LLMs take the learned route, with lightweight selector that must run before attention; at long context it, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) [Liu et al., 2025] is the attention mechanism of DeepSeek-V3.2 and of GLM-5, GLM-5.1 and GLM-5.2 [Zeng et al., 2026, Z.ai, 2026a,b]. Consider decoding token with tokens in the cache. At each layer lightning indexer with HI small heads scores every cached token L, It,n = HI(cid:88) h=1 wt,h ReLU(cid:0)qI t,h kI n,h (cid:1), (1) where It,n is the indexers score for query and cached token n, the superscript marks the indexers own projections (distinct from the layers attention), indexes its HI heads, and qI n,h are 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Long-Context Foundation Models. t,h, kI low-rank projections of the layer input with wt,h per-head weight. The layer keeps the set St of the k=2048 tokens with the highest score and runs attention over those tokens only. The selection is the sole coupling between the indexer and attention: attention cannot begin until the top-k is known, and nothing else in the layer depends on it. The two nevertheless run in sequence. Sparse attention gathers keys and its cost is flat in L; the indexer scans all keys. Beyond few tens of thousands of tokens the scan is the largest term on the attention side of the layer, two thirds of it at 128K (Figure 1). Only the selection dependency forces the order, and adjacent DSA layers select strongly overlapping sets (Section 2), cross-layer redundancy that reuse methods already exploit [Bai et al., 2026, Yang et al., 2025, Deshmukh et al., 2025], so layers attention need not wait for its own selection: an earlier layers serves. The cost of the indexer per decode step is product of two independent factors: how many indexers run, and how long each one is waited for. IndexCache [Bai et al., 2026] reduces the first, keeping the indexer on fraction 1/r of the layers (Section 2). We reduce the second. The Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) lets layer ℓ attend the selection produced by the previous indexer layer. The indexer of layer ℓ then feeds later layer, not its own attention, and the two run at the same time (in the idealized limit of Figure 1; the realized speedup is smaller, for reasons we trace in Section 5.2). Every selection is still recomputed at every decode step; nothing is reused across steps. Because the two factors multiply and neither method touches the others, the two remedies compose: on the layers IndexCache keeps, MLI hides the scan that IndexCache still pays. Like IceFormers deployable acceleration [Mao et al., 2024], MLI needs no retraining, applies to every DSA model, and leaves the selections unchanged. This is the regime long context forces: KV memory caps how many requests decode together (six at 128K, two at 195K on our node), so very long context is served few-at-a-time, exactly where the indexer scan is exposed; the gain fades only when many short requests pack the batch and saturate memory bandwidth (Section 5.2). Our contributions are the following. drop-in schedule that overlaps the indexer with attention. MLI (Section 3) makes layers indexer and its attention independent, at any retention and lag depth, so they run concurrently; it needs no retraining and no new weights, runs in SGLangs decode CUDA graph with the production kernels unchanged, and is faster still on DeepSeek-V3.2 with fused decode kernel (Section 5.3). Faster at equal retention, and one further halving for free. Serving DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM5 under IndexCaches protocol (Section 5.1), IndexCache+MLI decodes faster than IndexCache at the same retention: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4; and at retention 1/r it is faster than IndexCache at 1/2r while attending twice as many fresh selections, so halving of the indexer budget comes at no speed cost. At 128K it reaches 1.32 the unmodified models throughput at 1/4, above IndexCaches 1.28 at 1/8. shared-primitive fused kernel, and the case for co-design. On DeepSeek-V3.2 fused decode kernel runs the sparse attention and the indexers prefix scan of shared step in one launch, per-request win (Section 5.3); it does not help GLM-5, which has fewer index heads per rank. Because the indexer scores the same group bilinear interaction as attention, this is evidence that DSA models should be co-designed around that shared primitive: direction we argue for and partly realize, not model we train. The quality cost of staleness is small and recoverable. Across five long-context suites (Section 5.4), attending an older selection stays within few points of IndexCache at every retention it reports; the arm with twice the fresh selections, now the faster of the two, matches IndexCache on LongBench and LongBench v2 and is within 3 points on RULER (Section 5.6), and distilling only the indexers, applied identically to both methods, recovers little at the mild retentions IndexCache reports but rescues the collapse at aggressive retention (Section 5.5).

sections.title: 3.2 Realization inside the decode graph
sections.content: We implement Equation (2) in SGLangs DSA decode path; its portable realization changes no kernel (a fused kernel, faster on DeepSeek-V3.2, is Section 5.3), and Figure 2 shows one decode step. At full layer, as soon as the layer input exists, the indexer (its projections, the scan over the paged index-key cache, and the top-k) is enqueued on second CUDA stream while attention on the main stream proceeds with the selection that Equation (2) assigns to the layer. The second stream is joined at the layer that first consumes the new selection, full layers later, and references to the indexers inputs and output are held until that join so the allocator cannot reuse their memory. The cross-stream edges are ordinary graph dependencies, so the whole schedule is captured once into the decode CUDA graph and replayed without host involvement; per-layer registry carries selections between full layers, and shared layers receive the carried selection exactly as in IndexCache. Because the scan and the top-k are the production kernels on the production buffers, each full layer produces the selection the standard schedule produces; only the layer that consumes it changes.

sections.content: MLI changes exactly one thing, the selection layer attends, and the cost of that change can be paid back without touching the backbone. sections.title: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Models and serving. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 (61 layers, 128 attention heads, 64 indexer heads) and GLM-5 (78 layers, 64 attention heads, 32 indexer heads) from their fp8 checkpoints with SGLang v0.5.16 on one node of eight H200 GPUs, with 8-way tensor parallelism, an fp8 KV cache, CUDA graphs enabled for every arm and k=2048 (a data-parallel-attention replication is in Section F). Regimes and contexts. We report (i) per-request decode throughput at single concurrent request; (ii) full-KV-cache decode throughput, where the request set is sized to the servers KV capacity and every prompt is first warmed into the prefix cache so that the measured phase is saturated decode; and (iii) prefill latency. Contexts are 10K, 60K and 120K tokens on both models, plus 128K on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 195K (199,680 tokens) on GLM-5. Retention is uniform with {2, 4, 8, 16, 32} (IndexCache reports up to 1/8). On GLM-5 we also run IndexCaches published searched patterns (40 and 22 full layers of 78), with MLI applied to the same patterns. Protocol and fairness. Every arm of cell (one model, one regime, one context) runs in the same job on the same node, differing only in model-override flags, so speed difference reflects the mechanism and not the setup. Three controls guard the comparison. (i) Drift: the unmodified model is booted first and again last, and the cell is reported only if the two agree within 2% (observed within 0.4%). (ii) Engagement: every MLI arm must log, on every tensor-parallel rank, the marker that the overlapped path was captured into the decode graph, with no fallback marker (Section A). (iii) IndexCache parity: IndexCache runs through its own released layer-skip knobs, and as control its arms are also booted on the unmodified SGLang release in the same job, where our build matches the release within 0.2% on the base model and is 0.4 to 1.1% slower on the IndexCache arms (Section C), so the tables understate IndexCache by at most 1.1 percentage points. Distilled arms are always paired with IndexCache distilled by the same recipe on its own spans (Section 3.3). Measurement noise is in Section J, and paired bootstrap intervals for every quality contrast in Section I. Quality. All evaluations are served through the same endpoints, with greedy decoding, and every delta is against the unmodified model on the same job. LongBench [Bai et al., 2024]: eleven English tasks, 100 examples each, inputs middle-truncated to 250,000 characters, task-native metrics, macroaveraged. LongBench v2 [Bai et al., 2025]: multiple-choice accuracy on the full 503-question set, inputs middle-truncated to 120K tokens, the official prompt, answer budget and answer extraction, each models non-thinking chat format (Section H). RULER [Hsieh et al., 2024]: needle retrieval, variable tracking and common-word extraction at 4K to 128K tokens, the benchmarks own metrics. Needle retrieval: ten numeric needles in haystacks of 32K to 520K characters. Decode perplexity: perplexity of the models own greedy 512-token continuation after 4K to 64K tokens of GovReport text, five seeds; deviation in either direction is drift.

sections.title: 5.2 What limits the gain
sections.content: With every indexer retained (r=1) and one request, MLI raises decode throughput by 19.8 to 26.1% on DeepSeek-V3.2 (the fused kernel) and 14.4 to 16.8% on GLM-5 (the deferred stream) across 10K to 195K (Table 1, second row). The ceiling, obtained by removing every indexer that can be removed (IndexCache at 1/32 retains two), is +31% on DeepSeek-V3.2 and +24% on GLM-5 at the longest context, so MLI hides about four-fifths of the exposed scan on DeepSeek-V3.2 and about two-thirds on GLM-5. The first full layers scan stays serial (no earlier layer to overlap), so even the ceiling is not fully reachable. Two ablations  (Table 3)  rule out scheduling as the further limit: high-priority CUDA stream and deeper k=2 or 3 window both change nothing. What remains is memory bandwidth: the scan hides only in the HBM bandwidth attention and the feed-forward block leave idle, which is why the gain vanishes once requests saturate it (Table 5, 64 requests; not profiled directly).

sections.title: 5.3 A fused kernel where bandwidth allows
sections.content: MLI has two realizations, both attending the production top-k. The deferred stream changes no kernel and issues the next layers indexer on second CUDA stream; the fused kernel runs the sparse attention and the prefix scan of the shared step in one launch, so the scan never competes for SMs with separate launch. On DeepSeek-V3.2 the fused kernel is faster at every retention and context, by 4 to 6 percentage points (composition at 1/4, 128K: +32.3% against +27.5%), and Table 1 uses it there. On GLM-5 it loses 2 to 4 percentage points to the deferred stream, which Table 1 uses instead: GLM-5 has half as many index heads per rank and smaller per-layer feed-forward window, so the single launch cannot hide the scan. sections.title: 5.4 What MLI costs
sections.content: The only behavioral change is which selection layer attends. Table 2 pairs the two methods at the retentions IndexCache reports, under the serving protocol where every retained layer computes its selection at prefill and copies only at decode (Section H). With every indexer retained, MLI alone is within 0.40.8 points of base on LongBench and LongBench v2, and on RULER 2.1 below on DeepSeek-V3.2 / 2.3 above on GLM-5, inside the models own base spread. Retention is cheap at 1/2 and 1/4: both arms stay within about 3 points of base on every suite. On top of IndexCache, MLI costs at most point or two  (Table 2)  ; the paired 95% intervals resolve differences that small only on RULER, spanning zero on LongBench and LongBench v2 (Section I).

sections.title: 5.5 Recovering it
sections.content: Distillation earns its place unevenly across the retention range, and where it does is exactly where the free halving matters most. At the mild retentions IndexCache reports the cost is already small, so distilling only the indexers (the recipe of Section 3.3, applied identically to both methods) has correspondingly little to recover and is neutral to slightly negative: distilled and undistilled arms are within 2.5 points of each other on LongBench and LongBench v2, and on RULER the distilled composition on DeepSeek-V3.2 sits 3 to 4 points below the unmodified model against 1 to 2 for distilled IndexCache (the intervals in Section exclude zero for the former and not the latter). At the cliff it is decisive: at 1/16 on GLM-5, distilling the indexers turns IndexCaches collapse (LongBench 11.5, RULER 61, needle 0.00) into recovery (LongBench 0.1, RULER 7.4, needle 1.00; Table 8), moving the usable range one halving further. Distillation swaps only indexer weights, so decode speed is unchanged. One mild-retention cell moves more (GLM-5 at 1/2 on LongBench v2, 2.5; single-seed swing).

sections.title: 5.6 At equal speed
sections.content: The halving pair no longer runs at equal speed (the composition at 1/r is the faster arm; Table 1), and it gives up nothing in quality to buy that speed: both arms sit within few points of base, and every 95% interval spans zero (Section I, Table 9) except one RULER pair on DeepSeek-V3.2 (3.1, [5.9, 0.6]). So within the retentions IndexCache reports the extra freshness comes free; one halving beyond, at the cliff (Section 5.5), it also avoids collapse, as IndexCache degenerates at 1/16 on GLM-5 and 1/32 on DeepSeek-V3.2 while the composition one halving above does not  (Table 8)  . These are single runs.

sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: Sparse attention and selection. Fixed-pattern sparse attention [Child et al., 2019, Beltagy et al., 2020, Zaheer et al., 2020] attends static subset; the learned variants adapt it: NSA [Yuan et al., 2025], MoBA [Lu et al., 2026], InfLLM-V2 [Zhao et al., 2026] and SeerAttention [Gao et al., 2024] learn to select blocks or tokens, DSA [Liu et al., 2025] with per-layer lightning indexer; Quest [Tang et al., 2024] estimates importance from cached key statistics and MInference [Jiang et al., 2024] from offline-assigned per-head sparse patterns; eviction and offloading [Zhang et al., 2023, Xiao et al., 2024, Li et al., 2024, Zhu et al., 2025, Luo et al., 2025] shrink or relocate the cache rather than the read; and Sadhukhan et al. [2026] argue that at test time sparse attention sets the cost per token. All of these run selection before attention. Distillation into sparse attention has targeted whole attention layers [Sundarapandiyan et al., 2025]; we distill only the indexers of model that already is sparse, toward its own selections. IndexCache [Bai et al., 2026] shares one DSA layers selection with neighbouring layers; TidalDecode [Yang et al., 2025] and Kascade [Deshmukh et al., 2025] reuse attention-derived selections across layers in models without an indexer. These reduce how often selection runs; MLI reduces how long layer waits for it, and composes with them. Selection and attention as one primitive. Attentions logit and the indexers score are both lowrank bilinear interactions of the layer input, so the indexer is second consumer of what attention already computes. Selective Attention [Leviathan et al., 2025] makes related point at training time: reusing attentions own scores as the selection signal rather than separate module. MLI exploits only the cross-layer overlap of the resulting selections, but our serving results argue for the tighter co-design: on DeepSeek-V3.2 single fused kernel computes the attention and the indexer scan in one launch. Training model whose indexer and attention share that primitive from the start is the natural next step.

sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.content: The gain of MLI falls with the number of requests decoding together. The fused kernel helps only DeepSeek-V3.2; on GLM-5 it loses to the deferred stream (Section 5.3). We evaluate GLM-5 as the familys representative: GLM-5.1 shares its base model and DSA architecture (only the checkpoint differs), so our results carry over; GLM-5.2 ships IndexCache natively as IndexShare, so comparison there would not be on equal footing and we leave it out of scope.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: DSA places lightning indexer in front of every attention layer, and the indexer scan is serial dependency of the step it feeds. It need not be. Adjacent DSA layers select almost the same tokens, so layer can attend the selection an earlier indexer already produced and run its own scan alongside attention rather than before it. The change is drop-in: no retraining, no new weights, and it composes with IndexCache. Serving DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5, it makes IndexCache faster at every retention, by up to 14.5% in decode throughput where the indexers are densest, and buys further halving of the indexer budget for free, since at half the retention the composition is already faster than IndexCache while attending twice as many fresh selections. The indexer only recomputes the bilinear interaction attention already forms, so the scan is not separate cost to hide but second reader of one primitive; the step this invites is to co-design DSA around that primitive rather than place selector ahead of it.

sections.title: I Confidence Intervals for the Quality Contrasts
sections.content: Tables 10 and 11 give paired bootstrap 95% intervals for every quality contrast the text makes: each arm against the unmodified model, IndexCache+MLI against IndexCache at equal retention, and IndexCache+MLI at 1/r against IndexCache at 1/2r (equal speed). The resample is over examples and is applied to both arms of contrast, so the interval is for the paired difference; intervals marked exclude zero.

sections.title: J Measurement Noise and Compute
sections.content: Three sources of variation bound every speed number. Within boot: repeating the per-request measurement five times on one warm server gives standard error of 0.01 to 0.03 tok/s per arm, so the equal-retention gaps carry 95% intervals of about 0.1 percentage point (DeepSeek-V3.2 at 128K: 1/4 +4.70 0.11, 1/8 +2.36 0.14; GLM-5 at 195K: 1/4 +4.12 0.06, 1/8 +2.61 0.06). Between boots in cell: the closing run of the unmodified model is within 0.4% of the opening one in every certified cell. Between cells: each replicate cell and its sweep cell, run on different days and nodes, differ by 0.8% (DeepSeek-V3.2) and 0.1% (GLM-5) on the unmodified model and by up to 0.5 and 0.2 percentage point on the equal-retention gaps. The between-cell figure is the one to read against the tables; the equal-retention margins at 1/2 to 1/8 exceed it several times over. All experiments ran on nodes of eight H200 GPUs (141 GB each) on an internal Slurm cluster. The reported speed sweep (20 cells plus 4 data-parallel and 2 replicate-CI cells, at 2 to 4 node-hours each) is about 90 node-hours; the quality matrix (48 arms) about 75; and distillation (18 runs) about 70. Including the fused-kernel realization and cells voided by the gates, the project used roughly three times the reported compute.

The KL term alone leaves the ranking near the selection boundary free; the listwise term fixes it there. Only the lightning indexers of the retained (full) layers are trained; the backbone, attention and the shared layers behavior are frozen. Teacher signal: the unmodified models indexer logits at the consumer layers, captured by forward hooks in frozen forward over the same input. For full layer ℓ with next full layer ℓ, the consumers are layers ℓ+1, . . . , ℓ1 under MLI (each attends (ℓ) one full layer late) and ℓ, . . . , ℓ1 under IndexCache (the retained layer also serves itself); the student at ℓ is trained against every consumer in its span, with the same per-consumer weight. Objective: 0.5 KL between the consumers softmaxed teacher scores and the students, plus 0.5 listwise PlackettLuce likelihood of the teachers top-2048 ordering under the student (the hybrid objective), 512 query rows sampled per step, causal masking. Data: GovReport documents packed into 8 streams of 32,768 tokens (DeepSeek-V3.2) or 16,384 (GLM-5). Optimization: 300 steps, AdamW, learning rate 103, no weight decay, gradient clipping at 1.0, seed 0, two H200 nodes per run. One run per (model, retention, span rule); the weights load at serving time through index_distilled_weights and change nothing else about the server.
